newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ may ease next week if jobs data soft-economists.
newsitem.headline: NZ may ease next week if jobs data soft-economists.

text.p: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand may ease monetary policy next week if Tuesday's employment data is soft, economists said on Friday.
In the first important release for the June quarter, Statistics NZ will publish Household Labour Force data at 2245 GMT on Tuesday.
Economists expect a slight contraction in employment and a rise in unemployment, adding to the picture of a weak economy.

They said the RBNZ's primary focus will be on the number of hours worked in the June quarter. The central bank has said it expects a significant rebound, because it believes March quarter data was artificially depressed by the timing of Easter.
RBNZ projections show the total number of hours worked rising a seasonally-adjusted 1.9 percent in the June quarter, against a 2.2 percent fall in the March quarter.
However, Bankers Trust NZ chief economist David Plank forecast hours worked would rise only 1.0-1.5 percent.
If so, the economy would be weaker in the first half of 1997 than the RBNZ thought, allowing the bank to accommodate a larger easing than it projected in June, he argued.
ASB Bank economist Anthony Byett agreed the RBNZ's forecast of a 1.9 percent rise in hours worked was unrealistic.
"I can't see it's going to be anywhere near that number. I haven't sat down and looked at it in depth, but I would expect it would be closer to zero than to 1.9 percent.

"Irrespective of whether they look at that figure, employment growth or the unemployment rate, I think there will be sufficient evidence that there is a weaker economy than the RB forecast. I believe they will ease," Byett told Reuters.
He said rather than wait until its September 18 economic projections, the RBNZ would sanction a further 50 basis point easing on Tuesday.

The RBNZ's optimum level for the Monetary Conditions Index (MCI) is 825 in the September quarter, moving to 785 in the December quarter. A one point move in the MCI equates to a one basis point move in the 90-day bank bill rate, and the RBNZ has
a comfort zone of 50 pips either side of its assumptions.
In Friday trade the MCI dipped below 735, more than 90 basis points easier than the RBNZ's desired level.
Byett said the market was building in an easing and by Tuesday expectations would be very high.
The RBNZ would have to make a statement either saying the market was too easy or sanctioning the move.
"I don't think they can afford to sit back, wait another three or four weeks and say let's do our numbers and see how it looks. I just don't think that does their credibility any good."

BTNZ's Plank said the timing of any easing would depend on the data. The bank's usual approach would be to wait until the quarterly economic projections, but a very weak employment report might prompt an easing after Tuesday's data, he said.
In the latter instance, the bank might lower its desired MCI to 775-800, but if it waited until September 18 it could be ease more aggressively, he added.

WestpacTrust economists said the currency was likely to come under further selling pressure if the data was weak. However, the data would have to be "significantly" different from forecasts to prompt the RBNZ into action next week, and it was
more likely to wait until its economic projections, they said.
Thirteen economists polled by Reuters expected on average seasonally adjusted employment to contract by 0.15 percent in the June quarter, following a 0.1 percent fall in March.
They saw the unemployment rate rising to 6.92 percent in the June quarter from 6.4 percent in March.
